# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This book explains what happens to sequencing data **after you hand your
libraries to the sequencing core**. It is for people who make libraries at the
bench and want to understand, step by step, how their FASTQ files become
count tables, genome-browser tracks and QC reports. You don't need any
background in programming or bioinformatics: the Foundations part starts
from "what is a terminal?" and "what is a `.gz` file?".

The first module covers **bulk RNA-seq**. Each chapter takes one processing
step, explains what problem it solves, shows the command, has you run it
yourself on a small practice dataset, and tells you how to judge whether it
worked. Everything runs on a laptop, a workstation or a computing cluster. The
steps follow [bagPipes](https://github.com/PhanstielLab/bagPipes) `RNApipe`, a
Snakemake pipeline (Trim Galore → Salmon + HISAT2 → deepTools → tximport), but
the ideas apply to any RNA-seq pipeline. Later modules will cover **ATAC-seq** and
**ChIP-seq / CUT&Tag / CUT&RUN** in the same way.

::: {.callout-note}
**This is a curriculum, not a manual.** It explains the *why* behind each
step, so any pipeline's documentation and output files make sense. For running
bagPipes itself, its [README](https://github.com/PhanstielLab/bagPipes) and code
are the reference.
:::

## What you will be able to do

By the end of the RNA-seq module you should be able to:

1. Use the shell to look inside any file in the pipeline, compressed or not,
   and say what each line and column means (FASTQ, FASTA, GTF, BED, bedGraph,
   bigWig, SAM/BAM).
2. Explain what each step is for, and name the common alternative tools
   (STAR vs HISAT2, Salmon vs kallisto, featureCounts) and what they assume.
3. Read a FastQC report and a MultiQC report and point out a problem.
4. Explain why reads are trimmed and what Trim Galore removes.
5. Describe the difference between **quantifying** reads against a
   transcriptome (Salmon) and **aligning** them to a genome (HISAT2), and say
   which output each one feeds.
6. Open a BAM file and a bigWig track in IGV and interpret what you see,
   including strand-specific tracks.
7. Fill in a samplesheet and config file, launch `RNApipe` on a cluster, check
   on it, and recover from a failed run.
8. Load the results into R with `tximport` or `tximeta` and start a DESeq2
   analysis.
9. Explain how processing changes for nascent-RNA assays such as TT-seq.

## The data, at a glance

What happens to your reads, file by file. Each box is a kind of file and each
arrow a tool (and a chapter):

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  FQ[("FASTQ.gz<br/>raw reads")] -->|"FastQC"| QC["QC report<br/>(HTML)"]
  FQ -->|"Trim Galore"| TQ[("trimmed<br/>FASTQ.gz")]
  TQ -->|"Salmon<br/>+ transcriptome index"| SF[("quant.sf<br/>per transcript")]
  SF -->|"tximport / tximeta<br/>+ GTF"| CM[("gene × sample<br/>counts")]
  CM -->|"DESeq2 (R)"| DE[("differential<br/>expression table")]
  TQ -->|"HISAT2 + samtools<br/>+ genome index"| BAM[("sorted BAM<br/>+ .bai")]
  BAM -->|"bamCoverage"| BW[("bigWig<br/>tracks")]
  BW -->|"IGV"| VIEW["look at<br/>the data"]
  QC & TQ & SF & BAM -.->|"MultiQC"| MQ["one QC<br/>report"]

  classDef file fill:#e8f1fa,stroke:#2c7bb6;
  class FQ,TQ,SF,CM,DE,BAM,BW file;
```

## How to use this book

- **On your own:** read the chapters in order. Each one ends with a short
  *Check your understanding* box; the answers are folded underneath.
- **In a group:** the [Teaching guide](teaching-guide.qmd) splits the module
  into sessions with hands-on exercises.
- **As a reference:** the [Glossary](appendix/glossary.qmd),
  [Command cheat sheet](appendix/cheatsheet.qmd) and
  [Troubleshooting](appendix/troubleshooting.qmd) appendices are meant for
  looking things up.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you need

- A computer running macOS or Linux (on Windows, WSL), with a terminal.
- About 2 GB of free disk for the practice data and the small (chr22)
  references, or ~30 GB for full human references.
- No special access: the practice data (four airway samples, GEO GSE52778) and
  the references (GENCODE) are public, and [Practice setup](rna-seq/practice-setup.qmd)
  downloads them for you. A computing cluster is only needed for the
  whole-pipeline chapter.

The companion guide [download-public-data](https://jpflores-13.github.io/download-public-data)
explains how to get any public dataset.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Boxes like this one are for UNC Longleaf / Phanstiel lab users

Folded boxes with this title give local shortcuts (prebuilt references, cluster

:::

## Conventions

- `Code in this font` is something you type, a file name, or a program name.
- Blocks with a grey background are commands. Lines that start with `#` are
  comments and are ignored by the computer.
- `$DATA`, `$REF`, `$WALK` are shortcuts to your practice folders, set up in
  [Practice setup](rna-seq/practice-setup.qmd#shortcuts-for-every-hands-on-box).
- `<something>` in angle brackets is a placeholder: replace it, brackets and
  all, with your own value.
- `{sampleName}` in curly braces is a placeholder that Snakemake fills in,
  for example `airway_ASM_N61311_untrt`.
- Tool versions quoted in this book come from `config/RNAconfig.yaml` in
  bagPipes (for example Salmon 1.10.3, HISAT2 2.2.1). Check your copy, because
  they change.
